clue.text: Beetle comes to have a lasting effect on Jack

parts.note: to scar is to leave a lasting mark on someone
a jack is a sailor, abbreviated AB (able seaman); 'on' places it after

explanation.surface: Something that leaves a lasting mark on a man called Jack, as if a beetle did it.
explanation.walkthrough: AB stands for able seaman, a common crossword stand-in for a sailor, and a jack (jack tar) is a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: The sacred dung beetle of ancient Egypt goes by this name.

clue.text: Though possibly heroic, he can't succeed on his own

definitions.text: he can't succeed on his own

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of the word heroic might be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A man may be brave, yet still can't get anywhere without help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' signals rearranging HEROIC. The definition is a cryptic description: someone who shares an inheritance cannot succeed to it alone.
explanation.definitionFit: One who inherits jointly with others shares the succession rather than taking it single-handed.

clue.text: Intervening between sides, aspire to wipe out this?

definitions.text: Intervening between sides, aspire to wipe out this?

indicators.note: intervening between says one piece sits inside the pair of letters for sides

parts.note: right and left sides, R and L

indicators.note: wiping out wrecks the word aspire, so its letters are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Someone stepping in to settle a quarrel hopes to end the cycle of revenge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to wipe out' is the anagram signal on ASPIRE. Read whole, the clue also describes what a peacemaker stepping between two sides hopes to abolish: retaliation.
explanation.definitionFit: Retaliation for a wrong is what a mediator between warring sides hopes to stop.

clue.text: Working well, obliged to take place at the top

indicators.note: in a down answer, at the top puts this piece first

parts.note: to be is to exist or take place
having to do something means being obliged to

explanation.surface: A machine functioning properly must sit at the top of its place.
explanation.definitionFit: A child or a machine that acts properly is said to be acting as it should; 'working well' covers both.

clue.text: Spectator's a weekly paper

explanation.surface: A reader reports that the Spectator is a weekly magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spectator is also a real British weekly, which tempts the solver to look for another magazine; the answer is the Sunday newspaper of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectator is an onlooker; the Observer is a British Sunday newspaper, published weekly.

clue.text: Workman cut by smug townsman

indicators.note: cut by says another piece slices into this one

parts.note: split as work plus man: a work is OP (opus), and Dan is an old title for a man, a master
pi, short for pious, means sanctimonious or smug

explanation.surface: A labourer is snubbed by a self-satisfied town dweller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Workman' has to be split into its parts. An oppidan is a townsman, and at Eton College the word means a boy who boards in the town rather than in college.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin oppidum, a town: the word names an inhabitant of a town.

clue.text: Unusual end of landscape by Constable, say

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: a special constable is a volunteer police officer, so a constable may be a special

explanation.surface: An odd corner at the edge of a landscape painted by John Constable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constable' looks like the painter, but it is the police rank: a special constable, a volunteer officer in Britain, is called a special.
explanation.definitionFit: Especial means exceptional or out of the ordinary, much like particular.

clue.text: Leaders given protection under covered wagon

indicators.note: in a down answer, under puts this piece below the other

parts.note: a van is a covered vehicle or wagon
a guard is a protection

explanation.surface: The front riders shelter under a covered wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: The vanguard is the foremost part of an army or movement, its leading people.

clue.text: Like a crop system requiring total rain and nothing artificial

indicators.note: artificial means made up, so the letters are put together in a new order

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A farming scheme that needs heavy rainfall and nothing man-made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'artificial' rearranges TOTAL RAIN plus O.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmers rotate crops field by field, so the system is described by this adjective.

clue.text: Police astride horses appearing promptly

indicators.note: appearing, with the plurals police and horses, says the mounted officer shows up more than once, so the unit is doubled
astride means straddling, so the police letters sit on either side of the horse

parts.note: a cop is a police officer
H is slang for horse (heroin); the plural horses gives two of them

explanation.surface: Mounted police arrive quickly on their horses.
explanation.walkthrough: The plurals do the work: police and horses both stand for two, so the policeman astride a horse appears twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Chop-chop is a colloquial order to hurry, meaning quickly or without delay.

clue.text: Old instrument in band without tuning peg

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the band goes round the peg

parts.note: a set is a group or band of people
a pin is the peg that holds and tunes a string

explanation.surface: A musician in a group lacks a peg for tuning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but means 'outside' here.
explanation.definitionFit: A small harpsichord of the 17th and 18th centuries is a classic early keyboard.

clue.text: Don't believe Duke is noble

parts.note: a count is a nobleman

explanation.surface: Doubting that a duke is truly aristocratic.
explanation.definitionFit: To discount a story is to dismiss it or refuse to credit it.

clue.text: Swede, say, about to join golf club shortly

indicators.note: to join says the abbreviation for about is attached to the end of the shortened club
shortly says the club's name is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a brassie is an old wooden golf club
ca, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: A Swedish golfer is about to join a golf club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swede' looks like a person from Sweden, but it is the root vegetable (rutabaga). A brassie is an old name for a two-wood golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: The cabbage genus includes the swede, an example of this plant group.

clue.text: Censor depressed writer

parts.note: feeling blue means feeling low or depressed
a pencil is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: A gloomy author suppresses the work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'writer' suggests a person, but it is the instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Editors struck out unsuitable text in blue crayon, so to blue-pencil is to cut or suppress words.

clue.text: University, with new advertisements, removes cause of stoppage

parts.note: plugs are pieces of publicity or adverts

explanation.surface: A university's new adverts are what finally clear a blocked system.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking out a bung or blockage clears the obstruction, as when a drain is freed.

clue.text: Only mineral water served in this interrogation cell?

definitions.text: Only mineral water served in this

parts.note: to pump someone is to question them persistently, so pumping is interrogation
a cell is a small room

explanation.surface: A grim interrogation cell where the prisoner gets only mineral water.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a prison cell; really it is a spa building where visitors drank the waters, as at Bath.
explanation.definitionFit: Spa towns had a hall where medicinal mineral water was dispensed to visitors.

clue.text: Peacemakers party outside normal working hours

parts.note: the UN (United Nations) sends peacekeeping forces
a social is a party or gathering

explanation.surface: A peacekeepers' get-together held late at night.
explanation.definitionFit: Shifts at night or weekends are called unsocial hours in Britain, being outside the usual working day.

clue.text: Champion gets youngster into trouble

indicators.note: into says the youngster goes inside the trouble

parts.note: pain means trouble or bother
a lad is a youngster

explanation.surface: A hero who gets a young lad into difficulties.
explanation.definitionFit: A knight of Charlemagne's court, hence any heroic champion of a cause.

clue.text: Water under the bridge? Quite the opposite

definitions.text: Water under the bridge? Quite the opposite

parts.words: Water under the bridge? Quite the opposite
parts.note: the idiom for past events is read literally and turned round: a bridge carrying the water over itself

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means old troubles best forgotten; flip it and you have a bridge with water on top.
explanation.definitionFit: This structure is a bridge carrying a channel of water across a valley.

clue.text: Somerset author's agent in colourless study

parts.note: ashen means pale or colourless
a den is a private room or study

explanation.surface: A spy from Somerset hides in a pale study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somerset' looks like the English county but is W. Somerset Maugham, whose spy stories feature a British agent of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Maugham's secret-agent hero, based on his own wartime intelligence work, carries this name.

clue.text: High Church feature

parts.note: High Church suggests a ritualistic branch of Anglicanism, but read plainly it is a tall part of a church building

explanation.walkthrough: High Church is a tradition in the Church of England; here 'High' just means tall.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall tower with a spire rising above a church is its loftiest part.

clue.text: Frank's girl nearly packed after first sign of trouble

definitions.note: read as 'frank is', with frank an adjective meaning candid

indicators.note: after puts the girl and the packed pieces behind the opening letter
the first sign of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: Ruth is a girl's name

indicators.note: nearly says the word loses its last letter

parts.note: packed means full

explanation.surface: Frank's girlfriend was almost crammed in at the first hint of trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a man's name but is the adjective meaning candid; 'Frank's' stands for 'frank is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being candid and open means telling things as they are, honest in speech.

clue.text: Beneficial because fully content

indicators.note: the content of the words is what they hold inside, so the answer sits within them

explanation.surface: Something is good for you because it is thoroughly satisfying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' looks like 'satisfied' but is a noun: what the phrase contains.
explanation.definitionFit: Something helpful or of practical value serves a good purpose.

clue.text: Elope with my excited sweetheart, one under firm control

indicators.note: excited means stirred up, so the letters of elope and my are jumbled

parts.note: the heart of sweet is its middle letter, E

explanation.surface: Run off with my thrilled sweetheart, who is kept on a short leash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' rearranges ELOPE + MY into EMPLOYE. 'sweetheart' is a standard crossword way of saying E, the centre of 'sweet'.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm here is a company, and a member of staff works under its direction.

clue.text: Fudge that's used in American biscuit

parts.note: to fudge figures is to cook them, falsify them
ie (id est) means that is

explanation.surface: Fudge that goes into an American biscuit recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fudge' looks like the sweet, which fits the biscuit picture, but it is the verb meaning falsify.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US a small sweet baked biscuit has this name.

clue.text: Fruit useless for a pudding

parts.note: a plum is a fruit
duff is British slang for useless or broken

explanation.surface: Fruit that is no good for making a dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: Plum duff is a traditional British boiled suet pudding with dried fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A boiled suet dessert studded with raisins is a classic British example.

clue.text: Soft and gentle as a woolly jumper

definitions.meaning: resembling a young sheep, a woolly animal that leaps

explanation.surface: A mild person is as soft as a knitted sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'woolly jumper' looks like a knitted pullover; it is a young sheep, which jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Meek, docile people are often compared to young sheep.

clue.text: Ravel's complicated mass

definitions.meaning: read as 'ravel is', a ravel being a knot or snarl
a confused, knotted mass of threads or hair

explanation.surface: The composer Ravel's intricate Mass setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ravel' suggests the French composer and 'mass' a church setting; really a ravel is a snarl of threads.
explanation.definitionFit: A snarled knot of string or hair is an intricate muddle.
